cite_as: Hernandez, D. J. (2011). Double Jeopardy: How Third-Grade Reading Skills and Poverty Influence High School Graduation. Baltimore, MD: Annie E. Casey Foundation. ERIC ED518818.
claimed_finding: In a national longitudinal sample of 3,975 U.S. children born 1979-1989 (NLSY79 child data; reading measured with the PIAT Reading Recognition subtest), 16% of children not reading proficiently in third grade did not graduate from high school by age 19, versus 4% of proficient readers (about four times the rate); the rate was 23% for below-basic readers and 9% for basic readers. These are descriptive rates by reading group and poverty status, not regression-adjusted causal estimates.

cite_as: Lesnick, J., Goerge, R. M., Smithgall, C., & Gwynne, J. (2010). Reading on Grade Level in Third Grade: How Is It Related to High School Performance and College Enrollment? Chicago: Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago.
claimed_finding: Following a cohort of about 26,000 Chicago Public Schools third graders (ITBS reading), third- and eighth-grade reading scores were strongly correlated (r = 0.67); about 40% of students below grade level in third grade were also below grade level in eighth grade, and multilevel models controlling for demographics and third-grade school effects still showed eighth-grade reading differences between the below-, at- and above-grade-level groups.

cite_as: Lesnick, J., Goerge, R. M., Smithgall, C., & Gwynne, J. (2010). Reading on Grade Level in Third Grade: How Is It Related to High School Performance and College Enrollment? Chicago: Chapin Hall at the University of Chicago.
claimed_finding: In the same Chicago cohort, nearly 80% of students reading above grade level in third grade graduated high school within five years, compared with 60% of at-grade-level and 45% of below-grade-level readers. However, once eighth-grade reading, ninth-grade school and ninth-grade course performance were added to multilevel models, third-grade reading level no longer independently predicted graduation; only being above grade level still predicted college enrollment among graduates.

cite_as: Harding, J. F., Herrmann, M., Hanno, E. S., & Ross, C. (2019). Using Kindergarten Entry Assessments to Measure Whether Philadelphia's Students Are On-Track for Reading Proficiently. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic / Mathematica, Institute of Education Sciences. ERIC ED599402.
claimed_finding: For School District of Philadelphia students who took the Pennsylvania Kindergarten Entry Inventory in fall 2014/15 and the grade 3 PSSA in ELA in 2017/18, the KEI Emerging Academic Competencies score correlated 0.42 and Learning Engagement Competencies 0.32 with grade 3 PSSA ELA scores; higher KEI scores predicted grade 3 proficiency, but a threshold index correctly classified only 53% of proficient and 73% of non-proficient students.

cite_as: Harding, J. F., Herrmann, M., Hanno, E. S., & Ross, C. (2019). Using Kindergarten Entry Assessments to Measure Whether Philadelphia's Students Are On-Track for Reading Proficiently. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic / Mathematica, Institute of Education Sciences. ERIC ED599402.
claimed_finding: In the same Philadelphia cohort, students' spring AIMSweb reading scores correlated with their grade 3 PSSA ELA scores at 0.50 in kindergarten, 0.53 in grade 1, 0.73 in grade 2 and 0.72 in grade 3, so the association between early-grade reading screening and the grade 3 state test strengthened from kindergarten to grade 3 (unadjusted pairwise correlations).

cite_as: Schlesinger, M., Saleet, G., Stewart, K., & Mosher, K. (2021). Four-year analysis of 2015-16 Kindergarteners' aimswebPlus reading and PSSA performance from 2015-16 to 2018-19. School District of Philadelphia, Office of Research and Evaluation.
claimed_finding: Among 4,194 Philadelphia students followed from fall of kindergarten (2015-16) to the grade 3 ELA PSSA (spring 2019), students on average ended third grade in the same aimswebPlus performance group they started in; students later scoring Advanced, Proficient, Basic and Below Basic on the grade 3 PSSA had average fall-kindergarten aimswebPlus national percentile ranks of 72, 55, 41 and 29 respectively (descriptive, no covariate adjustment).

cite_as: Jordan, E., McKenzie, S. C., & Ritter, G. W. (2018). Long-Term Outcomes of Low-Achieving Third Grade Readers. Arkansas Education Report, 16(3). Office for Education Policy, University of Arkansas.
claimed_finding: Following three cohorts of Arkansas public school students from third grade (2008-09 to 2010-11) into high school, only 11.5% of students designated low-achieving readers in third grade (roughly the lowest-scoring 20-25% on the state reading test) caught up to the state average by high school, defined as scoring at the state average across grades 8, 9 and 10; catching up was less common for Black, Hispanic, male and economically disadvantaged students.

cite_as: Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., Pagani, L. S., Feinstein, L., Engel, M., Brooks-Gunn, J., Sexton, H., Duckworth, K., & Japel, C. (2007). School Readiness and Later Achievement. Developmental Psychology, 43(6), 1428-1446. ERIC EJ779938.
claimed_finding: Using six longitudinal data sets and regression models that mostly control for pre-school-entry cognitive, attention and socioemotional skills and family background, school-entry math, reading and attention skills were the strongest predictors of later reading and math achievement; a meta-analysis of the results ranked early math first, then early reading, then attention, while socioemotional behaviors were generally insignificant predictors.

cite_as: Herbers, J. E., Cutuli, J. J., Supkoff, L. M., Heistad, D., Chan, C.-K., Hinz, E., & Masten, A. S. (2012). Early Reading Skills and Academic Achievement Trajectories of Students Facing Poverty, Homelessness, and High Residential Mobility. Educational Researcher, 41(9), 366-374. ERIC EJ987215.
claimed_finding: In a longitudinal study of 18,011 students grouped by socioeconomic risk (homeless or highly mobile, free meals, reduced-price meals, neither), first-grade oral reading ability, together with risk status, predicted growth in reading and math achievement in grades 3 through 8; risk status predicted achievement beyond early reading scores and moderated how strongly first-grade oral reading predicted later reading growth.

cite_as: Juel, C. (1988). Learning to Read and Write: A Longitudinal Study of 54 Children from First through Fourth Grades. Journal of Educational Psychology, 80(4), 437-447. ERIC EJ389953.
claimed_finding: In a small longitudinal study of 54 children followed from grade 1 through grade 4, poor first-grade readers almost invariably remained poor readers at the end of grade 4, and early reading ability predicted later ability better than early writing skill did.

cite_as: Lacoe, J., & Steinberg, M. P. (2019). Do Suspensions Affect Student Outcomes? Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 41(1), 34-62. ERIC EJ1204837.
claimed_finding: Using student panel data from the School District of Philadelphia with student fixed effects and instrumental variables based on the district-wide change in suspension policy, a suspension decreased math and reading achievement for the suspended student; exposure to peers' suspensions for serious misconduct had very small negative spillovers on peer achievement and did not change peer absences.

cite_as: Steinberg, M. P., & Lacoe, J. (2017). The Academic and Behavioral Consequences of Discipline Policy Reform: Evidence from Philadelphia. Washington, DC: Thomas B. Fordham Institute. ERIC ED598616.
claimed_finding: After Philadelphia's 2012-13 code-of-conduct change limiting suspensions for low-level conduct infractions, students who had received a conduct suspension in the pre-reform year had 1.45 fewer absences in the following year than never-suspended students, but showed no change in achievement (difference-in-differences); the reform did not durably reduce conduct suspensions, and never-suspended peers in schools that did not fully comply saw a 0.06 SD decline in math achievement (peers in fully complying schools saw no change).

cite_as: Lacoe, J., & Steinberg, M. P. (2018). Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes. Peabody Journal of Education, 93(2), 207-227. ERIC EJ1179434.
claimed_finding: A district-level difference-in-differences analysis of Philadelphia's 2012-13 discipline reform found only a modest decline in suspensions for nonviolent infractions in the reform year, no change in total suspensions, an increase in serious incidents, an increase in the truancy rate and a decline in district math and ELA achievement after the reform, a mixed result for reducing suspensions as a lever on attendance and achievement.

cite_as: Balfanz, R., Byrnes, V., & Fox, J. (2014). Sent Home and Put Off-Track: The Antecedents, Disproportionalities, and Consequences of Being Suspended in the Ninth Grade. Journal of Applied Research on Children, 5(2), Article 13. ERIC EJ1188519.
claimed_finding: In a statewide Florida cohort of 181,897 first-time ninth graders (2000-01), the chance of graduating fell from about 3 in 4 to about one half with a first ninth-grade suspension and dropout chances roughly doubled; in logistic regressions controlling for demographics, attendance and course performance, each additional ninth-grade suspension lowered the odds of graduating by 20% and of enrolling in postsecondary education by 12% (correlational, not causal).

cite_as: Bacher-Hicks, A., Billings, S. B., & Deming, D. J. (2019). The School to Prison Pipeline: Long-Run Impacts of School Suspensions on Adult Crime. NBER Working Paper No. 26257.
claimed_finding: Using a sudden school-boundary change in Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools (plus a principal-switch design), students assigned to a middle school with a one-standard-deviation higher (stricter) suspension effect were 1.7 percentage points (15%) more likely to drop out and 2.4 percentage points (11%) less likely to attend a four-year college, and 15-20% more likely to be arrested and incarcerated as adults; the authors found no statistically significant impact on state test achievement.

cite_as: Sorensen, L. C., Bushway, S. D., & Gifford, E. J. (2021). Getting Tough? The Effects of Discretionary Principal Discipline on Student Outcomes. EdWorkingPaper No. 20-216, Annenberg Institute at Brown University (published 2022 in Education Finance and Policy, 17(2), 255-284).
claimed_finding: Using linked North Carolina middle school, discipline and justice records (2008-2016) and variation in principals' propensity to remove students, harsher principals reduced reported minor misconduct but lowered high school graduation for all their students (about 2 percentage points from the 10th to 90th percentile principal, marginally significant); for students with minor infractions, the same switch raised absences by 0.5 days, lowered test scores by 0.02 SD and lowered graduation by 2.7 percentage points.

cite_as: Chu, E. M., & Ready, D. D. (2018). Exclusion and Urban Public High Schools: Short- and Long-Term Consequences of School Suspensions. American Journal of Education, 124(4), 479-509. ERIC EJ1186270.
claimed_finding: Using quasi-experimental methods and longitudinal data on New York City public high school students, suspended students had weaker attendance, course completion rates and standardized test scores, were more likely to drop out, and were less likely to graduate within 4, 5 or 6 years; the negative relationships persisted after accounting for pre-existing differences between suspended and non-suspended students.

cite_as: Anderson, K. P., Ritter, G. W., & Zamarro, G. (2019). Understanding a Vicious Cycle: The Relationship between Student Discipline and Student Academic Outcomes. Educational Researcher, 48(5), 251-262. ERIC EJ1220624.
claimed_finding: Using 10 years of student-level data from all Arkansas K-12 public schools and controlling for the type of behavioral infraction, exclusionary consequences were associated with worse test scores and more grade retention than less exclusionary consequences; however, sensitivity checks showed these relationships may still be driven by selection bias into consequence type, so the causal effect is uncertain.

cite_as: Hwang, N. (2018). Suspensions and Achievement: Varying Links by Type, Frequency, and Subgroup. Educational Researcher, 47(6), 363-374. ERIC EJ1189786.
claimed_finding: Comparing the same students across school quarters with different suspension experiences (achievement measured at 12 time points over 3 school years), multiple suspensions were associated with lower math and ELA achievement even after controlling for differences between students, with suggestive evidence of stronger associations for students at elevated risk of suspension.

cite_as: Noltemeyer, A. L., Ward, R. M., & Mcloughlin, C. (2015). Relationship between School Suspension and Student Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. School Psychology Review, 44(2), 224-240. ERIC EJ1141532.
claimed_finding: A meta-analysis of 53 cases from 34 studies (1986-2012) found a significant inverse relationship between school suspensions (in-school and out-of-school) and academic achievement and a significant positive relationship between suspensions and school dropout, with the size of the relationships varying by suspension type and study or participant characteristics; the pooled studies are mostly correlational.
